items.title: Longshore drift can move entire beaches kilometres

options.text: It moves sand directly out to deep water

Waves hit at an angle so swash carries sediment up the beach at that angle; backwash returns it straight down under gravity — net transport is along the coast, building spits and tombolos, stripping beaches downdrift of groynes
It transports sediment upstream in estuaries

items.reveal:
Spurn Head (East Yorkshire) is a 5 km spit built by longshore drift carrying sediment south from the eroding Holderness cliffs (retreating up to 2 m/year). The cliffs supply around 1 million m³ of sediment annually — much of it eventually ends up on Spurn or in the Humber estuary.

Groynes trap drift on their up-drift side. The downdrift side is starved of sediment, accelerating erosion. Coastal management at one beach can damage another — sediment budgets are zero-sum.

Dawlish Warren (Devon), Hurst Castle Spit (Hampshire), Slapton Sands (Devon) all illustrate dynamic spit-and-bar systems.
items.why: Coastal protection in one place can damage another. Understanding sediment budgets and littoral cells is essential to avoid simply moving the erosion problem along the coast.

items.title: 36 biodiversity hotspots hold around 50% of plant species

options.text: Regions with at least 1,500 endemic vascular plants and at least 70% original habitat loss — 36 defined globally by Conservation International, holding around 50% of plants and 43% of vertebrates
Only the Amazon and Congo basins

items.reveal:
Norman Myers identified the concept in 1988; Conservation International refined it. The 36 hotspots include Madagascar, the Atlantic Forest of Brazil, the Mediterranean Basin, the California Floristic Province, Sundaland, and more.

Total hotspot area is now about 2.4% of Earth's land surface — and yet holds the indicated share of species. Original extents were around 16% of land surface; the rest has been lost to human use.

IUCN Red List, BirdLife International's Important Bird Areas and the Alliance for Zero Extinction overlay related conservation priority maps.
items.why: Conservation cannot save every place. Hotspot prioritisation is one — contested — way of allocating effort to where it can save the most species. The trade-off with savanna, boreal and ocean priorities is real.

items.title: The jet stream sits around 10 km above the surface

options.text: A surface wind near the equator
A narrow band of fast westerly winds (often 100-300 km/h) at around 9-12 km altitude (the tropopause), driven by temperature contrasts between polar and tropical air masses
An ocean current in the Pacific
A jet of supersonic air over deserts

items.reveal:
The polar jet (UK weather) and subtropical jet are the major Northern Hemisphere features. They meander in Rossby waves, and the shape of those waves controls where storm systems track.

Jet streams were discovered by Japanese balloon-bombing campaigns of WWII and by US bomber crews over the Pacific (1944) flying west into apparently impossible headwinds.

Arctic amplification (warming of the Arctic at roughly 4x the global rate) reduces the temperature contrast that drives the polar jet, possibly causing it to meander more — linked to more persistent weather extremes.
items.why: Surface weather has upper-atmosphere causes. Understanding why summer 2022 had heat domes or 2013-14 had stuck storm tracks requires looking at the jet.
